prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of accuracy and stability.

statement.case_for: I keep B042 as my preferred configuration, unchanged in names, and I have sharpened the citation after the chair's question. The point of separation from 2005 and 2012 is the lattice clock itself. A frequency comb is a ruler for optical frequencies and a single trapped ion is a single quantum absorber. Katori's magic-wavelength idea makes it possible to hold a very large number of neutral atoms tightly, in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil shifts, while the light shift of the trap cancels to first order on the clock transition. Interrogating many atoms at once is what changes the stability: the quantum projection noise of the measurement falls with the number of atoms, so averaging times for reaching the 1e-18 level shrink from weeks to hours. That is the decisive step, and neither the comb nor the single-ion clock offers it. Ye's group then showed that the combination of this scheme with an ultrastable laser and careful control of systematic shifts realises the 1e-18 regime, with clock comparisons that test relativistic redshifts over millimetre scales. The result is mature, reproduced by independent laboratories, and the attribution is two names with identifiable roles. After reading all eight statements I find nothing that changes the scientific ranking.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness remains that a sceptic can read the lattice clock as a very good engineering of tools honoured in 2005 and 2012, and Mehlig makes the sharper form of that point: Ye's record accuracy leans on comb technology and on ultrastable lasers. I answer that the citation must be anchored on the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme, not on optical frequency metrology as a whole, and I accept that this narrows what the two names can be credited for. A second weakness is credit beyond the two names: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others made real contributions, and I have not verified the early proposal record in detail, so I treat that as an open point and not a settled one. If the committee found that the early priority sits elsewhere, my preferred configuration would have to be reconsidered.

responses.point: Eriksson treats B042 as his first alternative and not as his preferred prize. He agrees the magic-wavelength idea is a distinct invention, but argues that the redefinition of the second has not happened, so recognition could wait without loss; he prefers DMFT (B033).
responses.response: I accept that the idea is distinct, and I appreciate that you discount your own field proximity to DMFT. I do not accept the timing argument. The redefinition of the second is a metrology-policy decision, taken by an international body, and its date depends on comparison campaigns and on consensus about several species. The science that the prize would recognise, the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at 1e-18, is already confirmed in several laboratories and does not need the redefinition to be true. Linking the prize to a policy step would make our decision depend on a process that we do not control. On B033 I agree with Olsson's reading in the chair summary that the credit for the first step, Metzner and Vollhardt, is an obstacle for this round, and that a method with a thin opening support should not outweigh a case supported by five members.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B019, with B042 as his fallback. He argues that the clocks refine a measurement paradigm already rewarded in 2005 and 2012, and that Ye's accuracy work leans on frequency-comb technology.
responses.response: The comb dependence is real and I will not deny it: every optical clock comparison uses a comb. But a prize is given for the decisive contribution, not for the absence of dependencies, and the same logic would deny most experiments that use a laser or a cryostat. The decisive contribution here is the magic-wavelength lattice, which turns an ion-clock-like environment into a many-atom clock, and that is what the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not cover. I therefore think your fallback is better described as a first choice for the committee as a whole. On B019, I agree that mechanism is not required for a discovery, as with superconductivity, and I withdraw the idea that an open pairing mechanism alone is a reason to wait. My remaining reason is the age of the field and the omitted junior experimentalists; those are a judgment about maturity, and I would like the committee to take them up again in a few years.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, prefers B042 with Katori and Ye and flags that Lemonde, Lisdat and Ludlow and the pending redefinition of the second remain open.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration, and I take your chair question about the many-atom stability as the one that matters. Stability and accuracy are different claims, and the citation should not blur them: the many-atom interrogation gives stability, and the control of lattice-induced and blackbody shifts gives accuracy at 1e-18. I would want the wording to say both. On priority, I cannot verify the early record and I would not want the committee to treat a two-name credit as proven before someone has checked it against the original proposals and first demonstrations. I would support an explicit statement in the minutes that this check is part of the final decision.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B042 in his round-1 statement, keeps the Higgs discovery (B057) as his first alternative, and calls the credit to the three founding leaders a policy choice about collaboration credit.
responses.response: I agree with you that B057 is the plainest discovery on the list, and I agree that the question is credit rather than physics. Since the chair asks whether the committee will adopt a convention, my view is that I do not see one that I can defend: crediting founding leaders reads as a leadership prize, and crediting the discovery analyses would exclude many with an equal claim. I therefore keep B057 as an alternative, not as a preferred configuration, and I ask the committee not to use it as a reason to postpone a case where the credit can be written cleanly.

uncertainties: I have not verified the documentary record on the early lattice-clock proposal and first demonstration, and whether Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto or others hold priority claims that a two-name credit cannot accommodate.

Whether the committee accepts that the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme is separable from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, as I argue, or reads the clock as an application of those results.
I have not checked current best uncertainty figures or the status of the redefinition of the second, so statements about 1e-18 rest on general knowledge and the candidate summaries.
Whether B057 would become the better choice if the committee adopted an acceptable convention for crediting large collaborations; I see none yet.
statement.conflict_note: I remain a Lund experimental atomic physicist and laser spectroscopist, working in a neighbouring field to the optical clock community. My profile documents a doctoral-period research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Hall's work belongs to the 2005 prize context that bears on B042, and I note that this proximity might be read as a tie to the lattice-clock community, although I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. My Lund colleagues, WACQT management and Deep Light Vision are quantum-technology connections that bear on B038, so I would restrain from advocating B038 as my preferred part. After the round-1 discussion I still do not see a specific conflict that would require recusal on B042, and I leave this judgment to the committee.
